quiz.explanation: A test cannot control state it cannot see, and leaked state couples tests together.

code_smells.title: Comments That Say 'What'
code_smells.summary: Comments that repeat the code instead of explaining why.
code_smells.problem: When a comment narrates the code, it duplicates it, goes stale and signals names are unclear.
code_smells.bad_code:
# increment i by one
i += 1

# check if user is adult
if u.a >= 18:
code_smells.good_code: if user.is_adult():
fix: Rename to make the code self-explanatory.
Keep comments for why, not what.

quiz.question: Which comment is worth keeping?
choices: # add 1 to counter
# Retry: the payment API is eventually consistent after refunds
# loop over users
# end of function
quiz.explanation: Good comments capture reasons the code cannot express.

code_smells.title: Deep Nesting (Arrow Code)
code_smells.summary: Layers of nested if statements pushing code to the right.
code_smells.problem: Each nested condition adds a level to remember. The happy path gets buried.
code_smells.good_code:
def pay(order):
    if not order: return
    if not order.valid: return
    if not order.user.active: return
    charge(order)
fix: Use guard clauses and return early.

quiz.question: What technique flattens deeply nested conditionals?
choices: Guard clauses with early returns
More else branches
Longer variable names
Global flags
quiz.explanation: Handle the exceptional cases first and leave the main path unindented.

code_smells.title: God Class
code_smells.summary: One class that knows and does too much.
code_smells.problem: A class collects unrelated responsibilities until everything depends on it and nobody dares to edit it.
code_smells.bad_code:
class App:
    def login(self): ...
    def charge_card(self): ...
    def render_pdf(self): ...
    def send_email(self): ...
code_smells.good_code:
class Auth: ...
class Payments: ...
class Reports: ...
class Mailer: ...
fix: Move behavior to the objects that own the data.

quiz.question: Which principle does a God Class violate most directly?
choices: Single Responsibility
Liskov Substitution
Dependency Inversion
Interface Segregation
quiz.explanation: A class should have one reason to change.

code_smells.title: Dead Code
code_smells.summary: Code that is never executed but still has to be read.
code_smells.problem: Old branches, unused functions and commented-out blocks stay behind 'just in case'.
why_bad: Looks important so people maintain it.
code_smells.good_code: # deleted — git history keeps it
fix: Use coverage and linters to find unused code.

quiz.question: Why is it safe to delete commented-out code?
choices: It is never safe
Version control keeps the history
Comments are executed
Python needs it removed
quiz.explanation: Git remembers, so the working tree can stay clean.

code_smells.title: Misleading and Abbreviated Names
code_smells.summary: Names like d, tmp, data or mgr that hide meaning.
code_smells.problem: Readers must decode abbreviations and generic names, and names that lie are worse than none.
code_smells.good_code:
def total_price(unit_price, quantity):
    return unit_price * quantity

quiz.question: Which name is best for a list of overdue invoices?
choices: lst
data2
overdue_invoices
x
quiz.explanation: A good name tells the reader what and why without a comment.

code_smells.title: If/Elif Chains on Type
code_smells.summary: Branching on a kind or type code everywhere.
code_smells.problem: The same if/elif ladder appears in many places; adding a new kind means editing all of them.
code_smells.bad_code:
if shape.kind == 'circle': area = 3.14 * r * r
elif shape.kind == 'square': area = s * s
fix: Let each type own its behavior.

quiz.question: What does polymorphism replace in this smell?
choices: Repeated type-checking conditionals
Variables
Modules
Imports
quiz.explanation: Each class implements the same method, so callers just call it.

code_smells.title: Speculative Generality
code_smells.summary: Abstractions built for needs that never arrive.
code_smells.problem: Extra layers, hooks and parameters 'in case we need them' add complexity with no current benefit.
code_smells.bad_code: class AbstractPluginFactoryManager: ...   # one plugin exists
code_smells.good_code: def load_plugin(name): ...
fix: Generalise when the second case appears.

quiz.question: What does YAGNI stand for?
choices: You Aren't Gonna Need It
You Always Get New Ideas
Yield And Generate New Items
Yet Another Generic Name Index
quiz.explanation: Don't add what you don't need yet.

code_smells.title: Shotgun Surgery
code_smells.summary: One small change forces edits in many files.
code_smells.problem: A single concept is scattered, so changing it means touching a dozen places.
code_smells.bad_code: # changing the date format means editing 12 modules
code_smells.good_code: # one format_date() used everywhere
fix: Gather the scattered logic into one place.

quiz.question: A tiny change needs edits in many files. What is the cause?
choices: A concept's logic is spread out instead of centralised
Files are too short
Too many tests
Slow computers
quiz.explanation: Cohesion: things that change together should live together.

code_smells.title: Data Clumps
code_smells.summary: The same group of values always passed around together.
code_smells.problem: start_date, end_date or lat, lng appear side by side across many signatures.
code_smells.bad_code:
def book(start, end, ...): ...
def cancel(start, end, ...): ...
fix: Create a small object for the group.

quiz.question: If three values always travel together, what is likely missing?
choices: A class or value object
More comments
A global
A longer function
quiz.explanation: A named concept removes repetition and attracts related behavior.

code_smells.title: Hardcoded Configuration and Secrets
code_smells.summary: Passwords, keys and URLs written in source code.
code_smells.problem: Credentials committed to a repository leak and make every environment share the same values.
code_smells.bad_code:
API_KEY = 'sk-live-123456'
DB = 'postgres://admin:pw@prod/db'
code_smells.good_code:
import os
API_KEY = os.environ['API_KEY']
fix: Read from environment variables or a secret manager.

quiz.question: Where should an API key live?
choices: In source code
In environment/config outside the repo
In a comment
In the README
quiz.explanation: Keep secrets out of version control so they can differ per environment and stay private.

code_smells.title: Mutating Arguments
code_smells.summary: Functions that silently modify the objects passed in.
code_smells.problem: The caller's data changes behind its back, so results depend on call order.
why_bad: Hard to reason about and test.
code_smells.good_code:
def with_tax(items):
    return [{**i, 'price': i['price'] * 1.18} for i in items]
fix: Document it if mutation is intended.

quiz.question: What is the risk of mutating a list passed as an argument?
choices: It runs slower
The caller's data changes unexpectedly
Python raises an error
None
quiz.explanation: Hidden side effects make code unpredictable; prefer returning new values.

code_smells.title: Premature Optimization
code_smells.summary: Making code harder to read for speed nobody measured.
code_smells.problem: Complex tricks are added before knowing where the time actually goes.
code_smells.bad_code: # hand-rolled cache and bit tricks in a function called twice a day
code_smells.good_code: # write it clearly, profile, then optimise the hot spot

quiz.question: What should come before optimising?
choices: Guessing
Measuring with a profiler
Rewriting in C
Adding threads
quiz.explanation: Make it work, make it clear, then make it fast where measurements say it matters.

code_smells.title: Hidden Time Dependency
code_smells.summary: Calling datetime.now() deep inside logic, making tests flaky.
code_smells.problem: Hidden clock access means results change with the moment you run, so tests can't control time.
code_smells.bad_code:
def is_expired(item):
    return item.expires < datetime.now()
code_smells.good_code:
def is_expired(item, now):
    return item.expires < now
fix: Pass the time (or a clock) in.
Inject dependencies instead of fetching them.

quiz.question: How do you make time-dependent code testable?
choices: Sleep in tests
Pass the current time in as an argument
Use global state
Skip the test
quiz.explanation: Injecting the clock lets a test choose any moment.
